summary: This is a humorous April 1st memo that creates a new RFC subseries called IETF Statements of Boredom. It is a joke.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a joke paper that invents a new series for saying you are bored, written for April Fools' Day.

questions: what are ietf statements of boredom
subtitle: A humorous proposal for a new RFC category to express collective boredom with nothing.

tldr.problem: April 1st, 1993: The IETF had standards-track RFCs and informational RFCs, but no mechanism for expressing deep collective concern while saying absolutely nothing useful.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes a new category called IETF Statements Of Boredom (SOBs), requiring review by the IAB, IRSG, IESG, and even the Academie Francais. Once everyone approves by falling asleep, the document is discarded, creating a technical vacuum.
tldr.outcome: This April Fools' joke satirizes the RFC process itself, poking fun at how some documents convey no useful information while receiving full institutional review.

today: RFC 1438 is an April Fools' joke that never created an actual RFC category. It remains a humorous commentary on the formality of the standards process and the existence of documents that consume institutional effort while conveying minimal substantive value.

sections.title: The Problem with Nothing to Say
sections.content:
This is an April 1st joke document. The RFC jokes that while the IETF has two types of RFCs—standards-track documents and informational documents—it lacks a mechanism for publishing documents that express deep concern about something important but otherwise contain absolutely no useful information whatsoever.

The memo creates a fictional new RFC subseries: IETF Statements Of Boredom, or SOBs. The name itself is a humorous double entendre, playing on both "Statements of Boredom" and the conventional meaning of SOB as an acronym.
sections.plainLanguage: The joke says the IETF should make a special rulebook series for saying you are bored about something, but saying absolutely nothing else.

sections.title: The SOB Process
sections.content:
The RFC satirizes the official RFC approval process by describing the SOB review workflow: submission to the IAB, IRSG, IESG, and the SOB Editor (named Morpheus). The process includes review, analysis, reproduction in triplicate, and even translation into ASN.1 (a technical notation). The document must also go to the Academie Francais and be distributed to "Internet insomniacs."

However, once everyone has approved the document by "falling asleep over it," the process ends and the document is discarded. The resulting vacuum is "viewed as having the technical approval of the IETF, but it is not, and cannot become, an official Internet Standard."
sections.plainLanguage: Experts have to read and approve it, but then they throw it away. It gets approval to become nothing.

sections.title: Satire of the RFC Process
sections.content:
The RFC mocks the bureaucratic aspects of standards development by imagining a series that follows all the formal procedures of the standards track but produces nothing of value. The joke is that many RFCs receive serious review and approval while conveying little substantive information.

References to ASN.1 translation and the Academie Francais add absurdist humor, as does the mention of the "SOB Editor Morpheus." The security section playfully notes that security issues are not discussed—because "no other issues of any importance are discussed in this memo either."
sections.plainLanguage: It jokes that some official documents are boring and pointless, so there should be a special category for those.

references.text: Internet Activities Board, "The Internet Standards Process", RFC 1310, IAB, March 1992.
